evidence_quotes.quote: The survey revealed that 0.35 million rural households and 14,300 urban households did not have access to proper sanitation facilities and were practicing open defecation out of a total of 1 million households

Extant evidence clearly indicated that success of a sanitation program depended as much on behavioral change in every individual of the district as it did on mobilization of resources and quick service delivery.
Disclaimer. This case is written solely for educational purposes and is not intended to represent successful or unsuccessful managerial decision-making.
The planning and implementation of the program progressed over a span of 2 years during which 0.35 million sanitation facilities were built.
Increased and accelerated sanitation coverage from 60 to 97 per cent.

criterion_notes.c1: Yes. The paper examines household and community sanitation service access, specifically the construction of sanitary toilets and elimination of open defecation across rural and urban households, schools, and ICDS centres in Nadia District, West Bengal, India.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this would be 'yes' because the case describes administrative and institutional leadership by the District Magistrate's office, inter-agency coordination (MGNREGA, NRLM, NBA, ICDS, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan), and collaboration with block development officers and gram panchayats. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, however, Criterion 2 is 'no': the paper describes generic public-sector project delivery, inter-departmental resource mobilization, supply-side facilitation (rural sanitary marts and mason training), and CLTS/IEC behavioural promotion (seminars, school outreach, human chains, pledge declarations, and volunteer persuasion committees), rather than any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility rules, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariffs, discretion, regulatory enforcement, or utility structure).
criterion_notes.c3: No. Published in Emerald Emerging Markets Case Studies as a pedagogical teaching case explicitly written solely for educational purposes (with a disclaimer that names, financial, and recognizable information may have been disguised), the article reports no empirical research design, sampling, qualitative fieldwork methodology, or quantitative analytical methods, relying solely on narrative description and secondary summary statistics cited from project websites and external UNICEF/HIJLI reports.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes. The narrative cites secondary programme summary figures relevant to sanitation service access and coverage, including access to sanitary toilets for over 336,000 families (0.35 million sanitation facilities built), sanitation coverage increasing from 60% to 97%, and reported toilet usage increasing from 57% to 99.8%.
criterion_notes.c5: No. Although the target district population (5.2 million residents / 1 million households in Nadia District) and programme-level sanitation coverage indicators are stated, the publication is an educational teaching case with no identifiable empirical study design or research methods and no rule-type exposure variable.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. The full text is in English.

population_and_sample: Residents and households of Nadia District, West Bengal, India (5.2 million population across 1 million households, including 0.35 million rural and 14,300 urban households without proper sanitation at baseline; no primary empirical sample reported)
exposure: Sabar Shouchagar Project: district-led sanitation campaign combining inter-departmental resource pooling, rural sanitary marts, mason training, and community/IEC behavioural mobilization
outcome: Household and institutional sanitary toilet construction and coverage (increasing from 60% to 97%; 0.35 million facilities built; access for over 336,000 families) and reported toilet usage (57% to 99.8%)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). This article is a pedagogical management teaching case published in Emerald Emerging Markets Case Studies ('written solely for educational purposes', with a disclaimer that names and financial/recognizable details may be disguised) that contains no empirical research methodology, data collection procedures, or primary analysis, citing only secondary summary figures from programme websites and external validation reports. In addition, under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it also lacks an eligible rule-type mechanism (c2 = no), as the Sabar Shouchagar Project described is a generic public-sector project delivery, supply-facilitation, and IEC/community behavioural-promotion campaign rather than a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule governing sanitation access.
